title: Get started
text: An embedded engine for realtime views Documents in. Live views out. Append JSON, map it into groups, and read the current result. Foldlite DB maintains versioned reductions in a local database you can regenerate. Start with Python ↓ Explore the API 01 Append Any finite JSON value → 02 Map Emit a key and contribution → 03 Reduce Read the current group state Unreleased development API. Use the reviewed source branch below. The default branch and published packages may not contain every API shown. Install the development source Python 3.11 or newer is required. Install the optional numeric runtime to use the shared Rust/WASM reducers. The bundled WebAssembly artifact needs no Rust compiler at installation. git clone --branch api-native-prototype-2026-10-19 \ https://github.com/255BITS/foldlitedb.git cd foldlitedb python -m pip install '.[reducers]' The base package has no external runtime dependencies. Python ordered folds work without the numeric extra. A metric in a few lines The map sees a document and emits a group key plus a value. Mean() keeps the count and mean current as documents arrive. These examples start with a fresh metrics.db file. from foldlitedb import Database, Mean, View def measurements(document): yield document.payload["metric"], document.payload["value"] metrics = View("metrics", "1", measurements, Mean()) with Database("metrics.db") as db: db.register(metrics) documents = db.add_many([ {"metric": "loss", "value": 4}, {"metric": "loss", "value": 8}, ]) result = [(row.key, row.result) for row in db.rows("metrics")] assert result == [("loss", {"count": 2, "value": 6.0})] There are no required document names or positions. add_many returns the resolved documents in input order, including generated identities and source positions. Save those records outside the database if you need to regenerate it. Append freely. Name when useful. Use add(payload) for one JSON value. Every unnamed call appends a new document. Supply an optional unique name when identical retries should count once. with Database("metrics.db") as db: db.register(metrics) saved = db.add({"metric": "loss", "value": 3}, id="measurement-3") assert db.add(saved.payload, id="measurement-3") == saved assert db.get("measurement-3") == saved Documents are immutable: changing an existing name's contents raises DocumentConflict . Names are scoped to a source. For external logs, an explicit source and offset can supply the replay identity instead. Read once, follow changes rows handles ordinary reads with bounded snapshot pages. Use query when you also need a cursor for a change feed. with Database("metrics.db") as db: db.register(metrics) snapshot = db.query("metrics") fourth = db.add({"metric": "loss", "value": 1}) updates = db.changes("metrics", since=snapshot.cursor) assert updates.rows[0].result == {"count": 4, "value": 4.0} An append commits documents, checkpoints, view states, and change records together. Snapshot pages keep one committed prefix while new documents arrive. Keep exploring The Python API ↗ Appends, batches, rows, reducers, snapshots, and explicit control. Replay and ordering ↗ How identities, offsets, versions, and regeneration fit together. Structured state ↗ Track lifecycle state with a Python fold in ingestion order. Native experiments ↗ Explore Rust execution and storage work with explicit limits.

title: Python API
text: Reference · development API The Python API Start with add , add_many , and rows . Explicit documents and cursors are available when your application owns a log or a resumable feed. Database Database(path, *, generation="default", reset=False, max_batch=1024, max_batch_bytes=8 * 1024 * 1024, max_value_bytes=1024 * 1024, max_key_bytes=4096, max_page_bytes=8 * 1024 * 1024, max_emissions_per_document=1024, timeout=30) A local SQLite view cache, safe to share between Python threads. Separate instances and processes serialize writes through SQLite. Use a context manager or call close() . generation identifies the source collection. A conflicting generation requires an explicit reset=True , which discards derived storage and invalidates existing instances and cursors. Retain authoritative documents before resetting. Limit Meaning max_batch Maximum documents in one atomic ingestion call. max_batch_bytes Encoded payload, document-ID, and source bytes per batch; also bounds pending map values. max_value_bytes Encoded payload, contribution, reducer-state, and finalized-result size. max_key_bytes Encoded canonical JSON key size; cannot exceed 4096. max_page_bytes Total key, state, and result bytes in a returned page. max_emissions_per_document Bounds map output for each document. timeout SQLite lock wait in finite seconds, from 0 to 2147483.647. Adding documents add db.add(payload, *, id=None, source="default", position=None) → Document Append any finite JSON value. Omitted IDs are generated; omitted positions start at zero or follow the source checkpoint. The returned payload is a separate JSON value, isolated from caller and mapper mutations. An identical named retry reuses its original position. A source and position can also identify an identical unnamed retry. Conflicting identity reuse raises DocumentConflict ; a new document behind its source checkpoint raises SourceOrderError . add_many db.add_many(payloads, *, source="default") → tuple[Document, ...] Eagerly consume one bounded iterable of JSON payloads and append it atomically. Every member is one payload, so an array is kept whole. Results preserve input order and have generated IDs and consecutive source positions. Empty input returns () . Input errors, map failures, limits, and position exhaustion roll back the entire batch. Retrying this unnamed call adds another batch. Replay retained documents with ingest . Explicit documents and batches Document(id, payload, position, source="default") db.ingest(documents) → IngestResult db.ingest_many(documents, *, batch_size=None) → iterator[IngestResult] ingest atomically commits a bounded batch of explicit Document records. Identical replay performs no map work and must match the ID, position, and payload. Its result has inserted , replayed , and the committed ingestion sequence . ingest_many is lazy: iteration commits separate bounded batches. The default batch size is max_batch ; a failure preserves previously committed batches. Views and reducers View(name, version, map, reducer, references={}) db.register(view) → revision A map receives a Document and yields zero or more (key, contribution) pairs. Keys and values may be structured finite JSON. Each key owns a reducer state. The view version identifies map behavior; references declares captured external-input versions. Register callbacks on every instance that reads their views. Registration reuses compatible persisted state or rebuilds a changed definition atomically. Query and change reads catch registered callbacks up after another connection ingests documents. Numeric reducers Mean(*, runtime=None, positioned=False) Sum(*, runtime=None, positioned=False) Count(*, runtime=None, positioned=False) Envelope(*, runtime=None, positioned=False) RustReducer(name, *, runtime=None, positioned=False) The named constructors use the same descriptors and state formats as their explicit reducer IDs. They load the optional runtime when computation needs it. Ordinary maps emit finite numbers or null; null contributes nothing. Constructor Reducer ID Result Mean() mean/v1 {"count": n, "value": mean} ; empty value is null. Sum() sum/v1 Count and sum; empty sum is zero. Count() count/v1 Count and count value; counts non-null numeric emissions. Envelope() envelope/v1 Count and first/min/max/last points, each with value and position. Map a document to 1 to count it. Envelope order uses source positions plus deterministic identity/emission tie breaking. positioned=True accepts explicitly positioned portable contributions; it is intended for adapters that already own that position schema. OrderedFold OrderedFold(initial, step, *, version, finalize=None) A trusted Python fold for structured state. step(state, contribution) returns the next finite JSON state. Steps run in persisted ingestion order within a key. Ordered folds do not declare arbitrary partial-state merging. from foldlitedb import Database, OrderedFold, View def statuses(document): yield document.payload["record"], document.payload["status"] status = View("status", "1", statuses, OrderedFold(None, lambda previous, value: value, version="1")) with Database(":memory:") as db: db.register(status) db.add_many([ {"record": "a", "status": "open"}, {"record": "a", "status": "closed"}, ]) assert list(db.rows("status"))[0].result == "closed" Rows, snapshots, and changes rows db.rows(name, *, key=<omitted>, limit=100) → iterator[Row] Lazily iterate a stable snapshot in bounded pages. The first iteration selects its committed prefix. limit controls page size, from 1 to 4096; it does not cap total results. No transaction or lock spans a yield to application code. Omit key for every group. Supplying any JSON key, including null, filters exactly. Keys follow canonical JSON lexical order. View rebuilds and compaction can expire a paused iterator. query db.query(name, *, key=<omitted>, limit=100, after=None, cursor=None) → Snapshot A snapshot contains rows , cursor , after , and complete . Continue pages with both the original cursor and the returned after . Each Row contains key , finalized result , reducer state , and ingestion sequence . changes db.changes(name, *, since, limit=100) → ChangePage Read committed key postimages after a snapshot or change cursor. A change page has rows , a continuation cursor , and complete . Continue using that page's cursor. Changes coalesce repeated updates to the same key within one transaction. A page can split a transaction; its cursor retains per-key progress. Empty maps still advance progress. Lookup and maintenance get(identifier, *, source="default") → Document | None Read a cached immutable document with a freshly decoded payload. checkpoint(source="default") → int | None Read the highest committed source position. refresh(name) Explicitly catch a registered view up to retained documents. Ordinary reads do this automatically. compact(name, *, before) Discard older change history while preserving the chosen snapshot boundary. The caller owns reader retention. stats() Return document, source, view, state, history counts and current ingestion sequence. Errors DatabaseError extends ValueError . Its specialized errors are DocumentConflict , SourceOrderError , CursorExpired , and GenerationMismatch . Failing callbacks propagate their exceptions and roll back their transaction. Missing numeric runtime support raises an actionable RuntimeError .

title: Replay and ordering
text: The model Replay and ordering Documents are immutable observations. Views are the changing state derived from them. Identities and positions make that state recoverable. Names are optional add(payload) assigns an internal ID. Two equal payloads still represent two observations. A caller-supplied name tells the database that a repeated call refers to the same observation. An identical named retry does no map work and keeps its original position, even after the source advances. Changing that name's payload is a conflict rather than an update. Model a changing lifecycle by appending a new observation and folding its status. Positions track a source A position means “this document's offset in its source.” Automatic positions start at zero and follow that source's committed checkpoint. External logs can supply their own monotonically increasing offsets, with gaps. from foldlitedb import Database, DocumentConflict, SourceOrderError with Database(":memory:") as db: first = db.add({"value": 4}, source="training.log", position=10) db.add({"value": 8}, source="training.log", position=40) assert db.add({"value": 4}, source="training.log", position=10) == first assert db.checkpoint("training.log") == 40 try: db.add({"value": 3}, source="training.log", position=30) except SourceOrderError: pass else: raise AssertionError("New records cannot arrive behind the checkpoint") IDs and positions are scoped to a source. A supplied source and position can identify a replay without a caller-supplied ID. An unseen record behind the checkpoint fails; a record at an already used position must match. Positions range from zero through 2**53 - 1 . Avoid mixing automatic positions with an external log's offsets unless they share the same progression. Ingestion order is separate Ordered Python folds process persisted ingestion order. A source offset does not sort records across sources, and a measurement timestamp does not reorder an existing fold. Applications choose the domain order before ingestion. Numeric envelopes use the declared source position plus a stable hash of source, document identity, and emission ordinal. This provides deterministic first/last ordering and min/max tie breaking, even when positions are equal across sources. Keep the source outside the cache The database file is derived storage. Retain resolved documents, exact map/fold behavior, reducer versions, and declared reference inputs outside it. from foldlitedb import Count, View count = View("count", "1", lambda document: [("all", 1)], Count()) with Database("live.db") as live: live.register(count) retained = live.add_many([{"value": 4}, {"value": 8}]) expected = list(live.rows("count"))[0].result # Retained records stand in for your application's authoritative archive. with Database("rebuilt.db") as rebuilt: rebuilt.ingest(retained) rebuilt.register(count) assert list(rebuilt.rows("count"))[0].result == expected Replay in original ingestion order. Keeping only payloads and generating new IDs can change identity-sensitive maps and numeric tie positions. An identifier for a lost taxonomy or snapshot does not reproduce its contents. Versions are promises A map's view version identifies its code and behavior. A fold has its own explicit version. Changing a callable, a captured input, or a reference version requires updating the declared definition. Compatible definitions reuse cached checkpoints. A different descriptor rebuilds that view atomically and invalidates its old cursors. Maps and folds are trusted application code, not a sandbox for arbitrary programs. Atomic commits and stable reads Each append batch commits document identities, source checkpoints, reduced states, and change records together. Failure rolls back the whole batch. Separate writers coordinate through SQLite. A snapshot cursor identifies a view revision and a committed ingestion prefix. Bounded pages retain that prefix while ingestion continues. Row iterators release transactions between pages; a sufficiently long pause may outlive your application's retained history. Compaction discards old changes under an explicit caller-selected boundary. It does not discard cached source documents needed for view rebuilds. Storage still grows with documents, distinct keys, and retained history. Numerical reproducibility Count and envelope states have exact merge contracts within their input bounds. Floating-point sum and mean use non-associative arithmetic: arbitrary merge trees need not produce identical bits. Native and WASM execution use the same Rust mathematical core. Preserve the declared order and partition plan when exact cross-runtime agreement matters. Do not merge finalized means; merge their compatible states with disjoint coverage. The JSON protocol preserves large finite floating-point states when they round trip through serialization. A bundled reducer update changes its module identity; compatible applications rebuild affected cached views and expire their old cursors through the normal view-version rules.

title: Native experiments
text: Engineering notes Native experiments Experimental Explore execution, data layout, and storage costs while preserving a clear reference contract. The Python API remains the supported starting point. The current path The Python database uses SQLite for document identity, ordered retention, state, history, and checkpoints. Trusted Python maps and ordered folds run in Python; bundled numeric reducers run the shared Rust core through WebAssembly. The unreleased convenience API changes how callers append and read. It does not silently select a new backend or promise parallel callback execution. A deliberately limited prototype The experimental engine runs native Rust with optional Python bindings, using the same reducer core across SQLite and a durable custom log. Its view contract is a single declarative numeric view over top-level fields, rather than arbitrary Python maps or ordered folds. Separate experiment. Backend compatibility, durability, worker ordering, and numerical behavior need explicit verification. Prototype throughput is not a performance promise for the full Python database API. Install the base development checkout first, then build the optional native package separately. This step requires a Rust toolchain; the ordinary Python/WASM installation does not. python -m pip install '.[reducers]' python -m pip install ./experimental/python from foldlitedb_experimental import NativeDatabase, NativeView metrics = NativeView("metrics", "metric", "value", reducer="mean/v1") with NativeDatabase("native.log", metrics, backend="log", workers=4) as db: retained = db.add_many([ {"metric": "loss", "value": 4}, {"metric": "loss", "value": 8}, ]) assert list(db.rows())[0].result == {"count": 2, "value": 6.0} with NativeDatabase("native.log", metrics, backend="log", workers=4) as db: assert db.ingest(retained).replayed == 2 snapshot = db.query() db.add({"metric": "loss", "value": 3}) assert db.changes(since=snapshot.cursor).rows[0].result == { "count": 3, "value": 5.0, } Choose backend="sqlite" for the experimental SQLite journal. The native query methods omit a view name because a database has one view. NativeView also accepts a version, synthetic map-work amount, and emission count for controlled experiments. Current limits Only numeric field projections and the mean, sum, count, and envelope reducers are supported. Python callbacks, ordered folds, multiple views, in-place view rebuilds, and compaction are outside this prototype. Rust document mapping and emission use 1–64 workers. Grouping and per-key reduction currently run serially and preserve contribution order. The default worker count follows available CPUs, capped at 64. The expanded batch of emissions is buffered before reduction. Up to 1024 documents with 1024 emissions each can require substantial memory; streaming backpressure and compact worker shards are not implemented. Both backends append commit records and maintain in-memory indexes. Reopening replays the full journal; memory and retained history grow with data. Both backends hold an exclusive process lock. This is not the production Python database's concurrent-reader deployment model. The experimental SQLite backend uses a journal-plus-memory layout, so storage comparisons do not isolate SQLite library overhead from all data-layout differences. Float-valued grouping keys, including floats nested in structured keys, use deterministic Rust JSON ordering that can differ from Python canonical JSON ordering because exponent formatting differs. Grouping and exact lookup still work; universal cross-engine row-order parity is not promised. Measured worker scaling Local medians from 156 fresh-process trials, with 2 repeats per configuration. The illustrated uniform workload has 4,096 documents, 128 keys, 512-document durable batches, and 8 live updates using mean/v1 . The host exposes 24 logical CPUs; storage is ext4 / /dev/mapper/nvme4tb . Ingestion timings exclude numeric runtime warm-up and include the same batch boundaries and durable acknowledgments. Within each matched workload, fixture and result hashes agree across engines and worker counts. Cheap field mapping Workers Native SQLite docs/s vs. 1 worker Native log docs/s vs. 1 worker 1 71,582 1.00× 72,002 1.00× 2 72,838 1.02× 74,964 1.04× 4 70,102 0.98× 73,277 1.02× 8 73,162 1.02× 73,858 1.03× 12 76,799 1.07× 75,263 1.05× 24 68,904 0.96× 75,437 1.05× Synthetic CPU-heavy mapping The artificial map performs 10,000 integer-mixing rounds per document. This measures available map parallelism, not an application speed guarantee. Workers Native SQLite docs/s vs. 1 worker Native log docs/s vs. 1 worker 1 33,543 1.00× 32,192 1.00× 2 44,420 1.32× 46,593 1.45× 4 54,858 1.64× 57,267 1.78× 8 62,924 1.88× 66,470 2.06× 12 66,808 1.99× 68,871 2.14× 24 67,607 2.02× 67,426 2.09× Cheap maps show no consistent multicore benefit. The synthetic case improves end-to-end ingestion by roughly two times, while its map phase scales further. Serial grouping, reduction, serialization, and commit costs remain. SQLite and the custom log are close in this fixture; neither is a categorical winner. Startup and memory remain part of the cost These one-worker rows use the cheap uniform workload. Setup includes explicit numeric runtime warm-up plus database opening; whole-process peak memory includes the Python host. The native backends replay their full journal on reopening. Engine Setup + warm-up Reopen + full query Peak RSS Storage Python / SQLite + WASM 67.22 ms 13.36 ms 82.2 MiB 668 KiB Native / SQLite 5.67 ms 8.37 ms 37.3 MiB 552 KiB Native / log 1.37 ms 9.45 ms 34.8 MiB 534 KiB No OS page-cache eviction was performed. These small, two-repeat measurements do not establish large-history reopen cost, bounded memory, or production latency. The Python/native comparison also changes data layout and algorithms; worker-count comparisons within one native backend isolate parallelism more closely. Download the complete NVMe/ext4 report for every distribution, individual sample, latency, phase cost, and source hash. The separate tmpfs run is supplementary CPU-oriented evidence and is not used in these storage tables. Payload size probe A separate 30-trial NVMe/ext4 probe adds unused ASCII padding of 0, 1 KiB, or 16 KiB per document while preserving numeric map results. Each configuration uses 512 documents plus 8 live records, 64-document durable batches, 128 keys, and two repeats. Compare sizes within this probe; its batch size differs from the worker-scaling matrix. Padding / document Python SQLite docs/s Native SQLite, 1 worker Native SQLite, 4 workers Native log, 1 worker Native log, 4 workers 0 B 5,031 38,219 39,102 41,660 40,202 1 KiB 4,736 26,932 29,268 31,304 32,499 16 KiB 3,296 4,884 4,883 6,324 6,936 Actual encoded fixture sizes, including identities and live records, are 47,880, 587,120, 8,574,320 bytes respectively. At 16 KiB padding, median whole-process peak RSS for one worker is Python: 97.9 MiB, native SQLite: 58.6 MiB, native log: 54.9 MiB. Larger ignored payloads exercise JSON serialization, validation, copying, retained storage, and durability together; these timings do not isolate one cause. Peak RSS also includes fixture objects, encoded input, and the Python host. This small padding probe does not establish behavior for every nested document shape or high-fanout map. Download the complete payload probe . The original 156-trial results remain unchanged, with their measured runner hash and source commit preserved in the primary report; the new padding option is additive and defaults to zero. Measure complete workloads The existing deterministic benchmark measures document construction, mapping, numeric reduction, transactions, queries, reopening, and regeneration: mkdir -p .benchmark-storage python scripts/benchmark_database.py \ --documents 100000 --keys 128 --batch-size 1024 \ --live-documents 100 --storage-root .benchmark-storage \ --output /tmp/foldlite-database.json Its initial ingestion includes lazy runtime compilation. Live operations reuse that instance; same-process reopening and regeneration reuse the compiled module but create fresh instances. Its “rebuild” timing means registering before ingestion, not rebuilding a view over an already retained history. Compare native and WASM execution with storage held constant, then compare storage with computation held constant. Report startup separately from warmed operation and match the durable acknowledgment boundary. Choose the filesystem you mean to measure explicitly: temporary directories can be backed by memory. Keep tmpfs results separate from measurements on a persistent storage device. The comparison matrix Dimension Cases to distinguish Data Low/high key cardinality; uniform, hot-key, and clustered distributions; small and nested payloads. Computation Count, envelope, sum, mean; cheap/expensive maps; zero, one, and many emissions. Execution Batch sizes; worker counts; native/WASM boundaries; queue and merge costs. Storage Durable SQLite and custom log with equivalent acknowledgment semantics; memory-only results reported separately. Lifecycle Historical registration, live reads, change feeds, restart, suffix catch-up, and regeneration. Evidence Throughput, latency distributions, total process memory, disk/log size, runtime versions, fixture hash, and numerical agreement. Correctness before speedups Out-of-order worker completion must preserve document and emission order where required. Duplicate, overlapping, missing, and retried worker ranges must not double-count or advance progress past unfinished work. Failure, cancellation, process exit, and torn writes must preserve the promised commit boundary. Snapshot pages and change feeds must expose committed prefixes and retain explicit cursor expiry. Count and envelope require exact agreement; sum and mean need a declared numerical contract and deterministic merge plan. Slow tasks and high-cardinality keys must not create unbounded queues or memory growth. Parallel key reduction and parallel mapping are different capabilities. Python ordered folds cannot use arbitrary partial-state merging. Any future fast path must state the semantics it supports.
